newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Former Secretary Baker blasts U.S. Mideast vetoes.
newsitem.headline: Former Secretary Baker blasts U.S. Mideast vetoes.

text.p: Former U.S. Secretary of State James Baker criticised the Clinton administration on Wednesday for having vetoed two Security Council resolutions last month calling on Israel to halt a new settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
"I am disappointed that my government saw fit to veto Security Council resolutions after standing up and saying that it opposed settlement activity," he said.

"It seems to me that those actions send very conflicting signals," Baker added, referring to Israel's plans to build 6,500 homes for Jews on a site between Jerusalem and Bethlehem captured in the 1967 Middle East war.

The United States said at the time that while it opposed the Israeli action, the United Nations was not the appropriate forum for dealing with issues that should be settled directly between the Israelis and Palestinians.

Baker, who was secretary of state when the Middle East peace process was launched at a 1991 Madrid conference and was a frequent critic of Israeli policy, was speaking to reporters during a visit to the United Nations.
He was recently appointed Secretary-General Kofi Annan's personal envoy for the Western Sahara, a territory disputed between Morocco and the Polisario independence movement.
Answering questions about the Arab-Israel dispute, Baker said: "I am disappointed, if I may say so, that we have let bombs and bulldozers drive the (Middle East peace) process."
Alluding to Palestinian suicide bombings and Israeli settlement building, he added: "There is no excuse for the bombs. But, in my view, there is also no excuse for the bulldozers.

"Because what has happened here, when you have settlement activity such as we are now witnessing, you foreclose the possibilities for negotiation. And you make, of course, a mockery of (Security Council) resolutions 242 and 338, which call for a resolution of this matter through the process of negotiations."

On the faltering Middle East peace process, he said: "I am really very disappointed in what has happened. On the other hand, I think you have to look at what has taken place since we were able in 1991 to get the parties to sit down face to face together in Madrid. A lot of progress has been made.

"There is a warm peace today between Israel and Jordan. That would not have happened without Madrid. It would not have happened without Oslo," he added, referring to the initial negotiations between Israel and the Palestinians," he said.
"In the medium to long term I remain rather optimistic that continued progress can be made towards peace in that part of the world which also deserves it and badly neds it."

Asked whether his U.N. appointment was a "comedown" for someone who was once White House chief of staff as well as secretary of state, he replied: "Absolutely not. I want to tell you, chief of staff of the White House is the worst job in the United States government.

"I think that people who are interested in promoting peace and democracy and freedom around the world ought to be available to serve when someone calls upon them to do so if they have the experience, and I think I have the experience."
